saints.name: Maria of Paris

summary.text: Maria Skobtsova was a poet, emigrant, mother and Orthodox nun whose Paris hospitality became a refuge during the Nazi occupation. She was imprisoned and killed at Ravensbrück.

blocks.text: Born Elizaveta Pilenko in Riga, she grew up near the Black Sea. Her father’s death precipitated a period of atheism and involvement in literary and political circles. After revolution, two marriages and emigration, she arrived in Paris in 1923. The death of her daughter Anastasia intensified her work among people in need.

blocks.text: Teva Regule’s 2018 sermon presents a recognizably complicated historical person: an educated intellectual, political activist, divorced woman and nun. It describes her Russian Student Christian Movement work and her Rue de Lourmel house as practical service rather than only discussion. She provided a fixed address needed for public assistance, cooked meals and offered counsel. During the occupation she helped Jewish people find safe places and assisted the resistance. The sermon locates her arrest within this wartime work and describes her continuing to share food and support fellow prisoners. Its interpretation is that of a named Orthodox preacher, distinct from the source’s biographical events.

blocks.text: She became a nun in 1932 with Metropolitan Evlogy’s support. Her houses served refugees, the homeless and the sick; she and Father Dimitri Klepinin later helped Jews obtain documents and escape routes.

blocks.text: The OCA dates her death in the gas chamber to March 31, 1945. It explicitly reports conflicting accounts: whether she was selected or took another prisoner’s place. The substitution story is therefore not presented here as settled fact.

blocks.text: The Archdiocese’s 2026 commemoration identifies her as poet, artist, revolutionary, nun, resistance worker and martyr. It records recognition extending beyond Orthodox circles: the 1982 film, Yad Vashem’s 1985 Righteous Among the Nations distinction, a Catholic Worker house named for her, and a Paris street named in 2016. It also notes the preservation of her memory by the Protection parish and cooperation with the Compiègne deportation memorial. These are later commemorations, not additional episodes of her wartime life. The same ecclesiastical source identifies her 2004 canonization and remembers her death on March 31.

blocks.text: Regule dates the Ecumenical Patriarchate’s canonization act to January 16, 2004 and connects the commemoration with other martyrs of the Russian emigration in France. Her sermon is linked to the act rather than replacing it with an app-written account of ecclesiastical authority.

blocks.text: The article also places her in the National Archives exhibition on women deported to Ravensbrück, held from February to June 2023. This contemporary museum context accompanies the Archdiocese’s account of continued parish remembrance and shows how her documented life is preserved through both church commemoration and the history of deportation.
